summary.text: The Black Death was a plague pandemic that swept through Europe from 1346 to 1353.
It was one of the most fatal pandemics in human history, killing up to 50 million people, around 30% to 60% of Europeans.
The disease was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is mainly spread by flea bites.

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: The bacterium Yersinia pestis, mainly spread by fleas

facts.label: Slow recovery
facts.value: Europe's population regained its 14th century level only in the 16th century

facts.label: English name
facts.value: "Black death" is first attested in English in 1755

items.prompt: Towns far inland caught the plague faster than rat fleas could have carried it. According to the evidence, what best explains this?

options.label: Black rats and their fleas moved overland as fast as ships
Winds carried the bacteria across the whole countryside
Marmots from Central Asia kept bringing it into Europe
Once ashore, it spread mainly from person to person

items.explain: There is evidence that, once ashore, it mainly spread person to person as pneumonic plague, which fits the quick inland spread. Fleas on rats were behind its travel by ship.

items.prompt: A historian traces how the plague reached Mediterranean ports in the 1300s. Which route does the account give?

options.label: Fleas on black rats aboard Genoese ships leaving Crimea
Hunter-gatherers walking from Lake Baikal into Europe
Along the old route of Justinian's plague from Pelusium
Chinese physicians sailing west with infected patients

items.explain: The pandemic reportedly reached Europe at the siege of the Genoese port of Caffa in Crimea, and was most likely carried by fleas on black rats on Genoese ships.

items.prompt: A chronicler writing in the middle of the 1300s sets down what is happening around him. What name would he most likely use for it?

options.label: The Black Death, as we say today
The Great Death, or a pestilence
The Second Plague Pandemic
The Plague of Justinian

items.explain: The 1347 plague was not called "black" in any European language at the time. Writers used words like pestilence and mortality, and most languages used a form of the Latin magna mortalitas, "Great Death".

items.prompt: Researchers confirmed in 2013 that Justinian's plague was caused by the same bacterium as the Black Death. How are the two pandemics labelled?

options.label: The Black Death is the first, Justinian's the second
Both are counted together as the first pandemic
Justinian's is the first, the Black Death tentatively the second
Justinian's is the first, the Great Famine the second

items.explain: Justinian's plague is known as the first plague pandemic, and the Black Death has been tentatively considered the second, even though they are 500 to 600 years apart.

items.prompt: A student asks why Europe's population was still below its 1300s level well into the 1500s. What reason does the account give?

options.label: A crisis of the late Middle Ages, with the Black Death and later outbreaks
Survivors fleeing in large numbers to the Middle East
Strict rules limiting marriage and having children
A warm climate that cut crop yields for generations

items.explain: The Black Death was the second great disaster of the late Middle Ages, after the Great Famine. Further outbreaks followed, and because of this crisis the population did not recover until the 16th century.

items.prompt: Researchers found plague DNA in the teeth of ancient hunter-gatherers buried near Lake Baikal. How do they think the disease first reached these people?

options.label: Fleas on black rats travelling on trade ships
Drinking water fouled by dead animals
Contact with raw organs or hides of infected marmots
Bites from lice carried in the clothing of travellers

items.explain: Researchers concluded the disease likely spread initially from marmots through contact with raw organs or infected hides, and then also passed between people through respiratory means.

paragraphs.heading: A pandemic of plague
paragraphs.text: The Black Death was an outbreak of plague that swept Europe between 1346 and 1353. Few pandemics in human history have been deadlier. It killed as many as 50 million people, somewhere between 30% and 60% of Europe's population, and about a third of the people of the Middle East. Its effects on population, the economy and culture reached far.

paragraphs.heading: The germ and how it spread
paragraphs.text: The disease came from a bacterium called Yersinia pestis. It passes mostly through the bites of fleas, but it can also travel through contact with infected tissue or body fluids. In its pneumonic form it also spreads through droplets in the breath. Once on land, the Black Death seems to have moved mainly from person to person in this pneumonic form. That would explain why it raced inland faster than rat fleas spreading bubonic plague could manage.

paragraphs.heading: From Crimea to the Mediterranean
paragraphs.text: Where the Black Death began is still argued over, with clues pointing to China, Central Asia, West Asia and Europe. According to reports, it first entered Europe in 1347, when the army of Jani Beg of the Golden Horde besieged Caffa, a Genoese trading port in Crimea. From there it was most likely carried by fleas on black rats aboard Genoese ships. It spread around the Mediterranean and into North Africa, West Asia and the rest of Europe by way of Constantinople, Sicily and Italy.

paragraphs.heading: Not the first plague
paragraphs.text: The Black Death is tentatively counted as the second plague pandemic. The first was the plague of Justinian, which struck from 541 to 549 and returned until 750; in 2013 researchers confirmed it was caused by Y. pestis. The bacterium itself appears to have evolved about 7,000 years ago, and strains carried by fleas appeared around 3,800 years ago. A 2026 study found its DNA in the teeth of 18 ancient hunter-gatherers near Lake Baikal in Siberia, with the earliest cases about 5,500 years old.

paragraphs.heading: A long aftermath
paragraphs.text: For late medieval Europe it was the second great natural disaster, after the Great Famine of 1315 to 1317. The plague kept coming back throughout the Late Middle Ages. Because of this run of crises, Europe's population did not climb back to its 14th-century size until the 16th century. Around the world, plague outbreaks went on returning until the early 19th century.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: People at the time did not call it black. Writers used Latin words such as pestilentia, meaning pestilence, and in English it was known as the great pestilence, the plague or the great death. Swedish and Danish chroniclers made "black death" its proper name in the 15th and early 16th centuries, and other languages then borrowed the phrase. English took it up only in the 1750s, with the first known use in 1755, as a translation of the Danish den sorte død.
